claim: Non-malignant breast epithelial cells cultured in three-dimensional laminin-rich extracellular matrix (lrECM) form well organized, growth-arrested acini.
source: Non-malignant breast epithelial cells cultured in three-dimensional laminin-rich extracellular matrix (lrECM) form well organized, growth-arrested acini, whereas malignant cells form continuously growing disorganized structures.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript (e.g., Petersen et al., 1992; Weaver et al., 1997).

claim: Malignant breast epithelial cells cultured in three-dimensional laminin-rich extracellular matrix form continuously growing disorganized structures.
source: Non-malignant breast epithelial cells cultured in three-dimensional laminin-rich extracellular matrix (lrECM) form well organized, growth-arrested acini, whereas malignant cells form continuously growing disorganized structures.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript (e.g., Petersen et al., 1992).

claim: Brief transient compression applied to single malignant breast cells in lrECM stimulated them to form acinar-like structures.
source: Here, we show that brief transient compression applied to single malignant breast cells in lrECM stimulated them to form acinar-like structures, a phenomenon we term 'mechanical reversion.'
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced colony size and organized structures after compression (Figure 1B-iii, Figure 1C, Figure 1E).

claim: Compression stimulated nitric oxide production by malignant cells.
source: Compression stimulated nitric oxide production by malignant cells.
evidence: Supported by DAF-FM DA fluorescence measurements showing increased NO production 30-60 min after compression (Figure 3C).

claim: Inhibition of nitric oxide production blocked mechanical reversion.
source: Inhibition of nitric oxide production blocked mechanical reversion.
evidence: Supported by experiments with L-NAME showing no reduction in colony size when NO production was inhibited (Figure 3F).

claim: Compression restored coherent rotation in malignant cells.
source: Compression also restored coherent rotation in malignant cells, a behavior that is essential for acinus formation.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data showing increased coherent rotation in compressed T4-2 cells (Figure 4B).

claim: Coherent rotation is essential for acinus formation.
source: Compression also restored coherent rotation in malignant cells, a behavior that is essential for acinus formation.
evidence: Based on previous work cited in the manuscript (Tanner et al., 2012).

claim: Acinar morphogenesis involves integration of both biochemical and biophysical cues.
source: Acinar morphogenesis involves integration of both biochemical and biophysical cues, the disruption of which can lead to malignancy (Bello-DeOcampo et al., 2001; Bissell and Hines, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Disruption of biochemical and biophysical cues in acinar morphogenesis can lead to malignancy.
source: Acinar morphogenesis involves integration of both biochemical and biophysical cues, the disruption of which can lead to malignancy (Bello-DeOcampo et al., 2001; Bissell and Hines, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Primary or non-malignant mammary epithelial cells form polarized, growth-arrested acini after 7 to 10 days in lrECM culture.
source: Under these conditions, primary or non-malignant cells form polarized, growth-arrested acini after 7 to 10 days in culture, whereas breast cancer cells grow continuously to form large disorganized colonies (Petersen et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Petersen et al., 1992 and confirmed by experimental data in this study.

claim: Breast cancer cells grow continuously to form large disorganized colonies in lrECM culture.
source: Under these conditions, primary or non-malignant cells form polarized, growth-arrested acini after 7 to 10 days in culture, whereas breast cancer cells grow continuously to form large disorganized colonies (Petersen et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Petersen et al., 1992 and confirmed by experimental data in this study.

claim: Normal or non-malignant breast epithelial cells grown on very stiff substrata form phenotypically malignant, non-polarized structures.
source: Normal or non-malignant breast epithelial cells grown on very stiff substrata form phenotypically malignant, non-polarized structures (Chaudhuri et al., 2014; Paszek et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Step compression of whole cartilage tissue increases interleukin expression.
source: Step compression of whole cartilage tissue increases interleukin expression (Murata et al., 2003), whereas dynamic compression of bone enhances bone remodeling (Chamay and Tschantz, 1972; Wolff, 1892).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murata et al., 2003.

claim: Dynamic compression of bone enhances bone remodeling.
source: Step compression of whole cartilage tissue increases interleukin expression (Murata et al., 2003), whereas dynamic compression of bone enhances bone remodeling (Chamay and Tschantz, 1972; Wolff, 1892).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chamay and Tschantz, 1972 and Wolff, 1892.

claim: The stress generated by the compressive strain relaxed within minutes.
source: Rheological measurements showed that the stress generated by the compressive strain relaxed within minutes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by rheological measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Uncompressed T4-2 colonies were disorganized and significantly larger than uncompressed S1 colonies.
source: We grew non-malignant S1 and malignant T4-2 cells in our deformable silicone wells without compression (Figure 1B–i,ii) and observed that uncompressed T4-2 colonies were disorganized and significantly larger than uncompressed S1 colonies that formed polarized acini (Figure 1C; analysis of variance, p=1.6×10−5), consistent with previous data (Petersen et al., 1992; Weaver et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C with statistical analysis (p=1.6×10−5).

claim: Compression of T4-2 cells at the single-cell stage led to a significant reduction in colony size 10 days later.
source: Surprisingly, compression of T4-2 cells at the single-cell stage led to a significant reduction in colony size 10 days later (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2I.

claim: Compressed S1 acini were not significantly different from uncompressed S1 colonies.
source: In contrast, compressed S1 acini were not significantly different from uncompressed S1 colonies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Compressed T4-2 colonies formed growth-arrested structures with a lower percentage of Ki67-positive cells than uncompressed T4-2 cells.
source: Consistent with phenotypic reversion, compressed T4-2 colonies formed growth-arrested structures with a lower percentage of Ki67-positive cells than uncompressed T4-2 cells (Figure 1D; t-test, p=0.012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis (p=0.012).

claim: Compression in the 3D-on-top geometry reduced the growth of malignant cells in a manner similar to that in the 3D embedded geometry.
source: We found that compression in the 3D-on-top geometry reduced the growth of malignant cells in a manner similar to that in the 3D embedded geometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 2J) and confirmed the statistical significance (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; paired t-test p=0.01).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2J and Figure 3F with statistical analysis (p=0.01).

claim: Compression of malignant MCF10A-CA1d cells showed a reduction in colony size.
source: After compression, malignant CA1d cells showed a reduction in colony size, whereas non-malignant MCF10A cells did not (Figure 1—figure supplement 4; paired t-test p=0.007 and p=0.29, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 with statistical analysis (p=0.007).

claim: Compression of non-malignant MCF10A cells did not result in a reduction in colony size.
source: After compression, malignant CA1d cells showed a reduction in colony size, whereas non-malignant MCF10A cells did not (Figure 1—figure supplement 4; paired t-test p=0.007 and p=0.29, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 with statistical analysis (p=0.29).

claim: Compression-induced phenotypic reversion is not unique to the HMT3522 series.
source: This result indicates that compression-induced phenotypic reversion is not unique to the HMT3522 series.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both HMT3522 and MCF10A cell lines showed similar responses to compression.

claim: At and above 15% of compressive strain, colonies decreased in size by about 25%.
source: Compression resulted in a threshold response: At and above 15% of compressive strain, colonies decreased in size by about 25% (Figure 2B; paired t-test, p=2.85×10−4) and had significantly fewer cells (Figure 2C; paired t-test, p=0.012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B with statistical analysis (p=2.85×10−4).

claim: At and above 15% of compressive strain, colonies had significantly fewer cells.
source: Compression resulted in a threshold response: At and above 15% of compressive strain, colonies decreased in size by about 25% (Figure 2B; paired t-test, p=2.85×10−4) and had significantly fewer cells (Figure 2C; paired t-test, p=0.012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis (p=0.012).

claim: The stiffness of lrECM did not significantly change under differential compressive strain (0.01% and 21.5%).
source: We found that the stiffness of lrECM did not significantly change (t-test, p=0.579, 0.699) and remained within the range reported for normal breast tissue (Chaudhuri et al., 2014; Paszek et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by rheological measurements with statistical analysis (p=0.579, 0.699).

claim: The stiffness of lrECM remained within the range reported for normal breast tissue.
source: We found that the stiffness of lrECM did not significantly change (t-test, p=0.579, 0.699) and remained within the range reported for normal breast tissue (Chaudhuri et al., 2014; Paszek et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by rheological measurements and citations to previous work.

claim: Responses to transient compression in this system were unlikely to be due to increased stiffness of the lrECM.
source: Therefore, any responses to transient compression in our system were unlikely to be due to increased stiffness of the lrECM.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that lrECM stiffness did not change with compression.

claim: Compression enhanced the formation of E-cadherin star patterns in malignant T4-2 cells.
source: In malignant T4-2 cells, compression enhanced the formation of E-cadherin star patterns (Figure 2D; analysis of variance p=3.58×10−4), demonstrating that compressed colonies exhibited morphologically 'normal' multicellular organization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis (p=3.58×10−4).

claim: Compressed colonies exhibited morphologically 'normal' multicellular organization.
source: In malignant T4-2 cells, compression enhanced the formation of E-cadherin star patterns (Figure 2D; analysis of variance p=3.58×10−4), demonstrating that compressed colonies exhibited morphologically 'normal' multicellular organization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of E-cadherin star patterns, which are characteristic of normal acini.

claim: Compression increased the frequency of lumen formation in T4-2 cells.
source: Quantification of lumen formation (example in Figure 2A at 23% strain), another feature of non-malignant acini, confirmed this result (Figure 2E; analysis of variance, p=0.0002).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E with statistical analysis (p=0.0002).

claim: Addition of exogenous nitric oxide to malignant T4-2 cells reverts the malignant phenotype.
source: Recent work has shown that the addition of exogenous nitric oxide (NO) to malignant T4-2 cells reverts the malignant phenotype (Furuta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Furuta et al., 2018.

claim: S1 cells produce endogenous NO in lrECM culture.
source: In contrast, S1 cells were found to produce endogenous NO in lrECM culture, and blocking NO production in non-malignant S1 cells could induce malignant behavior.
evidence: Supported by citation to Furuta et al., 2018 (implied from context).

claim: Blocking NO production in non-malignant S1 cells could induce malignant behavior.
source: In contrast, S1 cells were found to produce endogenous NO in lrECM culture, and blocking NO production in non-malignant S1 cells could induce malignant behavior.
evidence: Supported by citation to Furuta et al., 2018 (implied from context).

claim: Mechanical perturbations of other cell types in laminin-containing matrices are known to stimulate NO production.
source: Since mechanical perturbations of other cell types in laminin-containing matrices are known to stimulate NO production (Gloe and Pohl, 2002; Gloe et al., 1999; Rialas et al., 2000), we hypothesized that NO signaling may be the mediator of mechanical reversion.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Gloe and Pohl, 2002; Gloe et al., 1999; Rialas et al., 2000).

claim: DAF-FM DA fluorescence intensity increased nearly twofold 30–60 min after compression in compressed T4-2 cells relative to uncompressed cells.
source: We found that DAF-FM DA fluorescence intensity increased nearly twofold 30–60 min after compression in compressed T4-2 cells relative to uncompressed cells (Figure 3C; paired t-test, p<0.03), indicating that compression induced intracellular NO production in malignant cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis (p<0.03).

claim: Compression induced intracellular NO production in malignant cells.
source: We found that DAF-FM DA fluorescence intensity increased nearly twofold 30–60 min after compression in compressed T4-2 cells relative to uncompressed cells (Figure 3C; paired t-test, p<0.03), indicating that compression induced intracellular NO production in malignant cells.
evidence: Inferred from the increase in DAF-FM DA fluorescence, which is a sensor for NO.

claim: The difference in NO level was not detectable at 2 hr or 24 hr after compression.
source: This difference was transient; the difference in the NO level was not detectable at 2 hr or 24 hr after compression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The phenotypic shift observed in mechanically reverted acini was absent when NO production was inhibited with L-NAME.
source: Measuring colony sizes using bright-field images (Figure 3E) revealed that the phenotypic shift observed in mechanically reverted acini was absent when NO production was inhibited with L-NAME (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; paired t-test, p=0.01 and 0.97, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F with statistical analysis (p=0.01 and 0.97).

claim: Treatment of T4-2 cells with L-NAME for only 2 hr after compression was sufficient to abolish reduction in colony size.
source: Importantly, treatment of T4-2 cells with L-NAME for only 2 hr after compression was sufficient to abolish reduction in colony size (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; paired t-test, p=0.76).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F with statistical analysis (p=0.76).

claim: The addition of L-NAME to uncompressed T4-2 cells did not alter colony size.
source: The addition of L-NAME to uncompressed T4-2 cells did not alter colony size (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; paired t-test, p=0.82), whereas addition of an NO donor SNAP to uncompressed T4-2 cells reduced colony size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; paired t-test, p=0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F with statistical analysis (p=0.82).

claim: Addition of an NO donor SNAP to uncompressed T4-2 cells reduced colony size.
source: The addition of L-NAME to uncompressed T4-2 cells did not alter colony size (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; paired t-test, p=0.82), whereas addition of an NO donor SNAP to uncompressed T4-2 cells reduced colony size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; paired t-test, p=0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis (p=0.05).

claim: Replacing the medium with fresh medium without inhibitor 2 hr after seeding and lrECM polymerization (no compression) produced no measurable difference in colony size.
source: Furthermore, replacing the medium with fresh medium without inhibitor 2 hr after seeding and lrECM polymerization (no compression) produced no measurable difference in colony size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; paired t-test, p=0.39).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis (p=0.39).

claim: Supplementing only the starting medium with the NO donor spermine NONOate reduced colony size in uncompressed T4-2 cells.
source: Finally, supplementing only the starting medium with the NO donor spermine NONOate, which has a half-life of 40 min (Ramamurthi and Lewis, 1997), also reduced colony size in uncompressed T4-2 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; paired t-test, p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis (p=0.02).

claim: Compression induces a burst of NO production in malignant cells that promotes a phenotypically normal developmental program.
source: These results altogether suggest that compression induces a burst of NO production in malignant cells that promotes a phenotypically normal developmental program.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of increased NO production after compression and the requirement of NO for mechanical reversion.

claim: NO-mediated mechanical reversion requires only a transient signal to effect long-timescale phenotypic changes.
source: In contrast to chemical reversion, which often requires continuous drug treatment throughout the culturing period, NO-mediated mechanical reversion requires only a transient signal to effect long-timescale phenotypic changes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that 2 hr treatment with L-NAME was sufficient to block mechanical reversion, and that compression itself is transient.

claim: Non-malignant cells in lrECM rotate coherently in small clusters during the coordinated assembly of an organized, polarized acinus.
source: Non-malignant cells in lrECM rotate coherently in small clusters during the coordinated assembly of an organized, polarized acinus, but malignant cells do not, except when treated with chemical reverting agents (Tanner et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tanner et al., 2012.

claim: Malignant cells do not rotate coherently in small clusters, except when treated with chemical reverting agents.
source: Non-malignant cells in lrECM rotate coherently in small clusters during the coordinated assembly of an organized, polarized acinus, but malignant cells do not, except when treated with chemical reverting agents (Tanner et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tanner et al., 2012.

claim: Compression restored coherent rotation after the first mitosis in T4-2 cells.
source: Using time-lapse microscopy (Figure 4A), we observed that compression indeed restored coherent rotation after the first mitosis in T4-2 cells (Figure 4B, paired t-test p=0.009, Figure 4—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis (p=0.009).

claim: Compression did not detectably delay the time of first mitosis in T4-2 cells.
source: Time-lapse microscopy revealed that compression did not detectably delay the time of first mitosis in T4-2 cells (Figure 4C; paired t-test p=0.68).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4C with statistical analysis (p=0.68).

claim: The compression response is not likely the result of direct inhibition of proliferation.
source: Thus, the compression response is not likely the result of direct inhibition of proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that compression did not delay the time of first mitosis.

claim: Blocking the formation of E-cadherin cell-cell junctions blocked mechanical reversion.
source: Blocking the formation of E-cadherin cell-cell junctions blocked mechanical reversion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Applying compression 24 hr after seeding elicited no change in colony size.
source: Furthermore, applying compression 24 hr after seeding elicited no change in colony size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mechanical reversion is developmentally related to normal acinar morphogenesis and chemical reversion.
source: Our results indicate that mechanical reversion is developmentally related to normal acinar morphogenesis and chemical reversion, in that it requires formation of proper cell-ECM contacts leading to coherent rotation at the two-cell stage early in development of the tissue (Bissell and Hines, 2011; Fournier et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2004; Tanner et al., 2012; Wang et al., 1998; Weaver et al., 1997).
evidence: Inferred from the observations that mechanical reversion requires proper cell-ECM contacts and coherent rotation, similar to normal acinar morphogenesis and chemical reversion. Supported by citations.

claim: Mechanical reversion requires formation of proper cell-ECM contacts leading to coherent rotation at the two-cell stage early in development of the tissue.
source: Our results indicate that mechanical reversion is developmentally related to normal acinar morphogenesis and chemical reversion, in that it requires formation of proper cell-ECM contacts leading to coherent rotation at the two-cell stage early in development of the tissue (Bissell and Hines, 2011; Fournier et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2004; Tanner et al., 2012; Wang et al., 1998; Weaver et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that blocking E-cadherin prevents mechanical reversion and that compression restores coherent rotation. Also supported by citations.

claim: Mechanical reversion was observed only when compression was applied shortly after seeding.
source: Importantly, we observed mechanical reversion only when compression was applied shortly after seeding, and no response was observed to compression applied 24 hr after seeding.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No response was observed to compression applied 24 hr after seeding.
source: Importantly, we observed mechanical reversion only when compression was applied shortly after seeding, and no response was observed to compression applied 24 hr after seeding.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There exists a narrow window of time during which epithelial cell polarity is established once cells undergo their first division.
source: This finding is consistent with the existence of a narrow window of time during which epithelial cell polarity is established once cells undergo their first division (Tanner et al., 2012; Ragkousi and Gibson, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tanner et al., 2012 and Ragkousi and Gibson, 2014.

claim: The reversion was heterogeneous, possibly due to the inherent heterogeneity of tumor cells and lrECM, as well as the inhomogeneous nature of transient strain in the system.
source: This reversion was heterogeneous, possibly due to the inherent heterogeneity of tumor cells and lrECM, as well as the inhomogeneous nature of transient strain in our system.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on observed heterogeneity in the data.

claim: Transient compression triggered NO-mediated signaling that led to a sustained biochemical change.
source: Since the compression force rapidly dissipated (minutes timescale) and ECM stiffness remained unchanged during compression, we believe transient compression triggered NO-mediated signaling that led to a sustained biochemical change (Figure 4D).
evidence: Inferred from the observations that compression is transient, NO production is transient, but phenotypic changes are long-lasting.

claim: NO signaling sits at the intersection of the feedback loop between laminin in the ECM and p53, which is disrupted in malignant tissues.
source: Recent work in breast epithelial cells has shown that NO signaling sits at the intersection of the feedback loop between laminin in the ECM and p53, which is disrupted in malignant tissues (Furuta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Furuta et al., 2018.

claim: NO has been shown to inhibit malignant behavior via down-regulation of NFκB-mediated MMP-9 expression.
source: In other cell types, NO has been shown to inhibit malignant behavior via down-regulation of NFκB-mediated MMP-9 expression (Knipp et al., 2004; Sinha et al., 2006; Upchurch et al., 2001), inhibition of calcium-induced Ras/c-RAF/ERK1/2 pathway (Raines et al., 2004), and regulation of p53 activity (Forrester et al., 1996; Hofseth et al., 2003; Lala and Chakraborty, 2001; Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Knipp et al., 2004; Sinha et al., 2006; Upchurch et al., 2001).

claim: NO has been shown to inhibit malignant behavior via inhibition of calcium-induced Ras/c-RAF/ERK1/2 pathway.
source: In other cell types, NO has been shown to inhibit malignant behavior via down-regulation of NFκB-mediated MMP-9 expression (Knipp et al., 2004; Sinha et al., 2006; Upchurch et al., 2001), inhibition of calcium-induced Ras/c-RAF/ERK1/2 pathway (Raines et al., 2004), and regulation of p53 activity (Forrester et al., 1996; Hofseth et al., 2003; Lala and Chakraborty, 2001; Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raines et al., 2004.

claim: NO has been shown to inhibit malignant behavior via regulation of p53 activity.
source: In other cell types, NO has been shown to inhibit malignant behavior via down-regulation of NFκB-mediated MMP-9 expression (Knipp et al., 2004; Sinha et al., 2006; Upchurch et al., 2001), inhibition of calcium-induced Ras/c-RAF/ERK1/2 pathway (Raines et al., 2004), and regulation of p53 activity (Forrester et al., 1996; Hofseth et al., 2003; Lala and Chakraborty, 2001; Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Forrester et al., 1996; Hofseth et al., 2003; Lala and Chakraborty, 2001; Wang et al., 2002).

claim: NO at the appropriate intracellular concentration can serve as a 'native' reverting agent.
source: These findings suggest that NO at the appropriate intracellular concentration can serve as a 'native' reverting agent, and that mechanical stimulus by means of compression is one way to activate it.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that NO production is induced by compression and leads to phenotypic reversion.

claim: Mechanical stimulus by means of compression is one way to activate NO as a reverting agent.
source: These findings suggest that NO at the appropriate intracellular concentration can serve as a 'native' reverting agent, and that mechanical stimulus by means of compression is one way to activate it.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that compression induces NO production and phenotypic reversion.

claim: Other types of mechanical strains that stimulate nitric oxide production may also yield phenotypic reversion of malignant cells.
source: We anticipate that other types of mechanical strains that stimulate nitric oxide production (e.g. shear, stretch and etc.) may also yield phenotypic reversion of malignant cells.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observation that compression-induced NO production leads to reversion.

claim: Roles for regulated NO signaling in normal growth and morphogenesis have been reported in neurons.
source: Roles for regulated NO signaling in normal growth and morphogenesis have also been reported in neurons (Nikonenko et al., 2013), gametes (Gelaude et al., 2015; Jeseta et al., 2012), and vascular endothelial cells (Ramasamy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nikonenko et al., 2013.

claim: Roles for regulated NO signaling in normal growth and morphogenesis have been reported in gametes.
source: Roles for regulated NO signaling in normal growth and morphogenesis have also been reported in neurons (Nikonenko et al., 2013), gametes (Gelaude et al., 2015; Jeseta et al., 2012), and vascular endothelial cells (Ramasamy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gelaude et al., 2015 and Jeseta et al., 2012.

claim: Roles for regulated NO signaling in normal growth and morphogenesis have been reported in vascular endothelial cells.
source: Roles for regulated NO signaling in normal growth and morphogenesis have also been reported in neurons (Nikonenko et al., 2013), gametes (Gelaude et al., 2015; Jeseta et al., 2012), and vascular endothelial cells (Ramasamy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramasamy et al., 2015.

claim: In healthy cell types, a transient NO signal precedes a persistent asymmetry in cell morphology.
source: In these examples in healthy cell types, a transient NO signal precedes a persistent asymmetry in cell morphology.
evidence: Inferred from the cited examples of NO signaling in neurons, gametes, and vascular endothelial cells.

claim: In tumor cells, the roles of NO signaling vary widely with concentration, ranging from increasing proliferation and invasiveness to activating apoptosis and inducing resistance to therapeutics.
source: In tumor cells, the roles of NO signaling vary widely with concentration, ranging from increasing proliferation and invasiveness to activating apoptosis and inducing resistance to therapeutics (Dave et al., 2014; Fukumura et al., 2006; Krasnapolski et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2016; Ranganathan et al., 2016; Singh and Gupta, 2011; Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Dave et al., 2014; Fukumura et al., 2006; Krasnapolski et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2016; Ranganathan et al., 2016; Singh and Gupta, 2011; Thomas et al., 2008).

claim: A cell-ECM receptor is the key mechanosensory element in mechanical reversion.
source: With a role for NO signaling in ECM-to-nucleus communication, we hypothesize that a cell-ECM receptor is the key mechanosensory element in mechanical reversion.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the role of NO signaling and the requirement for cell-ECM contacts.

claim: NOS-1 binds to the cell membrane and forms a complex with the laminin receptor dystroglycan, the adaptor protein dystrophin and the actin cytoskeleton.
source: NO synthase 1 (NOS-1) binds to the cell membrane and forms a complex with the laminin receptor dystroglycan, the adaptor protein dystrophin and the actin cytoskeleton; this complex is essential for NO production by NOS-1 (Rando, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rando, 2001.

claim: The complex of NOS-1, dystroglycan, dystrophin, and actin cytoskeleton is essential for NO production by NOS-1.
source: NO synthase 1 (NOS-1) binds to the cell membrane and forms a complex with the laminin receptor dystroglycan, the adaptor protein dystrophin and the actin cytoskeleton; this complex is essential for NO production by NOS-1 (Rando, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rando, 2001.

claim: T4-2 cells express the proteins in the NOS-1/dystroglycan/dystrophin/actin complex, but NO production is impaired.
source: Although T4-2 cells express the proteins in the complex, NO production is impaired (Muschler et al., 2002), Furuta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Muschler et al., 2002 and Furuta et al., 2018.

claim: In T4-2 cells, the glycosylation of the extracellular domain of dystroglycan is aberrant.
source: In T4-2 cells, the glycosylation of the extracellular domain of dystroglycan is aberrant.
evidence: Implied from previous work cited in the manuscript (Muschler et al., 2002; Furuta et al., 2018).

claim: Transient compression promotes engagement of laminin and dystroglycan despite aberrant glycosylation.
source: We hypothesize that transient compression promotes engagement of laminin and dystroglycan despite aberrant glycosylation.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observation that compression induces NO production in T4-2 cells.

claim: The cell-ECM receptor dystroglycan itself would serve as a mechanosensor that drives downstream polarity.
source: In this way, the cell-ECM receptor dystroglycan itself would serve as a mechanosensor that drives downstream polarity.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the proposed mechanism of compression-induced laminin-dystroglycan engagement.

claim: In C. elegans, hemidesmosomes serve as mechanosensors that promote polarized epithelial morphogenesis.
source: A conceptually similar mechanism has been observed in C. elegans where hemidesmosomes serve as mechanosensors that promote polarized epithelial morphogenesis (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: Compressive force could alter secretion and degradation of matrix proteins.
source: Compressive force could alter secretion and degradation of matrix proteins (Cox and Erler, 2011; Lu et al., 2012) or directly induce integrin engagement (Katsumi et al., 2005).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on citations to previous work (Cox and Erler, 2011; Lu et al., 2012).

claim: Compressive force could directly induce integrin engagement.
source: Compressive force could alter secretion and degradation of matrix proteins (Cox and Erler, 2011; Lu et al., 2012) or directly induce integrin engagement (Katsumi et al., 2005).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on citation to Katsumi et al., 2005.

claim: Regulation of cell-cell signaling and apoptosis are not likely to be directly affected by compression in this assay.
source: Regulation of cell-cell signaling (Curry et al., 2005; van Es et al., 2005) and apoptosis (Cheng et al., 2009; Debnath et al., 2002), however, are not likely to be directly affected by compression in our assay because the timing of the compression, timescales of mechanical dissipation, and nitric oxide decay are much shorter than these processes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that compression and NO production are transient, while cell-cell signaling and apoptosis occur on longer timescales.

claim: Long timescale behaviors are altered by transient compression, so a mechanism by which some record of the compression event is stored must exist.
source: Long timescale behaviors are indeed altered by transient compression, so a mechanism by which some record of the compression event is stored must exist.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that transient compression leads to long-lasting phenotypic changes.

claim: NO may alter cell-cell or cell-ECM interactions via direct NO-mediated post-translation modifications such as nitrosylation.
source: One possibility is that NO alters cell-cell or cell-ECM interactions via direct NO-mediated post-translation modifications such as nitrosylation or directly activates or inactivates an intracellular signaling protein outside of the p53 pathway (Smith and Marletta, 2012).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on citation to Smith and Marletta, 2012.

claim: NO may directly activate or inactivate an intracellular signaling protein outside of the p53 pathway.
source: One possibility is that NO alters cell-cell or cell-ECM interactions via direct NO-mediated post-translation modifications such as nitrosylation or directly activates or inactivates an intracellular signaling protein outside of the p53 pathway (Smith and Marletta, 2012).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on citation to Smith and Marletta, 2012.

claim: The invasive behavior of a sheet of epithelial cells increases under constant compression perpendicular to the primary plane of the sheet.
source: Furthermore, it has been previously observed that the invasive behavior of a sheet of epithelial cells increases under constant compression perpendicular to the primary plane of the sheet (Tse et al., 2012), highlighting the importance of considering the direction, timescale, and biological context of a mechanical perturbation when observing a cell or tissue's response behavior.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tse et al., 2012.

claim: In endothelial cells, nitric oxide production is mechanically activated on millisecond timescales.
source: In endothelial cells, nitric oxide production is mechanically activated on millisecond timescales (Gloe and Pohl, 2002; Gloe et al., 1999), relaxing actomyosin contraction in nearby smooth muscle cells on sub-second timescales (Lincoln et al., 1994; Palmer et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gloe and Pohl, 2002 and Gloe et al., 1999.

claim: Mechanically activated NO relaxes actomyosin contraction in nearby smooth muscle cells on sub-second timescales.
source: In endothelial cells, nitric oxide production is mechanically activated on millisecond timescales (Gloe and Pohl, 2002; Gloe et al., 1999), relaxing actomyosin contraction in nearby smooth muscle cells on sub-second timescales (Lincoln et al., 1994; Palmer et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lincoln et al., 1994 and Palmer et al., 1987.

claim: The NO-mediated response in smooth muscle cells proceeds via nitrosylation of the heme group of soluble guanylate cyclase by an NO radical.
source: This response proceeds via nitrosylation of the heme group of soluble guanylate cyclase by an NO radical and is rapidly reversible when NO is depleted (Derbyshire and Marletta, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Derbyshire and Marletta, 2012.

claim: The NO-mediated response in smooth muscle cells is rapidly reversible when NO is depleted.
source: This response proceeds via nitrosylation of the heme group of soluble guanylate cyclase by an NO radical and is rapidly reversible when NO is depleted (Derbyshire and Marletta, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Derbyshire and Marletta, 2012.

claim: Epithelial cells exhibit increased contractility and malignant behavior in stiff microenvironments by activating Rac1 and PI3K signaling.
source: Epithelial cells exhibit increased contractility (Saez et al., 2005) and malignant behavior (Paszek et al., 2005) in stiff microenvironments by activating Rac1 and PI3K signaling (Chaudhuri et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Saez et al., 2005, Paszek et al., 2005, and Chaudhuri et al., 2014.

claim: Rac1 activity is regulated by NO via nitrosylation.
source: Interestingly, Rac1 activity is regulated by NO via nitrosylation (Raines et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raines et al., 2007.

claim: A critical balance between NO signaling and contractility may be necessary for normal acinar development.
source: We speculate that a critical balance between NO signaling and contractility may be necessary for normal acinar development, and that mechanical reversion restores this balance in malignant cells.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observations about NO signaling, contractility, and mechanical reversion.

claim: Mechanical reversion restores the balance between NO signaling and contractility in malignant cells.
source: We speculate that a critical balance between NO signaling and contractility may be necessary for normal acinar development, and that mechanical reversion restores this balance in malignant cells.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observations about NO signaling, contractility, and mechanical reversion.

claim: Breastfeeding has a protective effect against cancer.
source: This speculation grows more intriguing when considering the protective effect of breastfeeding against cancer (Veral et al., 2002) and the short timescale contractions of myoepithelial cells that surround the luminal epithelial cells during milk letdown (Adriance et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Veral et al., 2002.

claim: Myoepithelial cells that surround the luminal epithelial cells undergo short timescale contractions during milk letdown.
source: This speculation grows more intriguing when considering the protective effect of breastfeeding against cancer (Veral et al., 2002) and the short timescale contractions of myoepithelial cells that surround the luminal epithelial cells during milk letdown (Adriance et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adriance et al., 2005.

claim: A mechanically activated NO signal from the luminal epithelial cells may serve as an 'off' signal for contractility of the myoepithelial cells during milk letdown.
source: Could a mechanically activated NO signal from the luminal epithelial cells serve as an 'off' signal for contractility of the myoepithelial cells during milk letdown?
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observations about NO signaling and mechanical activation.

claim: Mechanical activity during breastfeeding may contribute to the protective effect of breastfeeding against cancer.
source: Could this mechanical activity be contributing to the protective effect of breastfeeding?
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observations about NO signaling, mechanical activation, and the protective effect of breastfeeding.

claim: A transient compression applied to single malignant cells embedded in a laminin-rich gel can lead to phenotypic reversion of malignant breast cells.
source: In summary, we find that a transient compression applied to single malignant cells embedded in a laminin-rich gel can lead to phenotypic reversion of malignant breast cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Compressed malignant cells show an increase in nitric oxide production relative to uncompressed malignant cells.
source: Compressed malignant cells show an increase in nitric oxide production relative to uncompressed malignant cells, and blocking NO production also blocks mechanical reversion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Blocking NO production blocks mechanical reversion.
source: Compressed malignant cells show an increase in nitric oxide production relative to uncompressed malignant cells, and blocking NO production also blocks mechanical reversion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Compressed malignant cells undergo coherent rotation at the two-cell stage.
source: Compressed malignant cells undergo coherent rotation at the two-cell stage and require E-cadherin function to achieve mechanical reversion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Compressed malignant cells require E-cadherin function to achieve mechanical reversion.
source: Compressed malignant cells undergo coherent rotation at the two-cell stage and require E-cadherin function to achieve mechanical reversion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transient forces are sensed through activation of NO signaling in the single cell, allowing activation of p53 and engagement of the normal morphogenetic program.
source: We propose that the transient forces are sensed through activation of NO signaling in the single cell, allowing activation of p53 and engagement of the normal morphogenetic program.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of compression-induced NO production, NO-mediated reversion, and the known role of NO in the laminin-p53 feedback loop.

claim: The stress in lrECM gels relaxed to zero with a characteristic time constant on the scale of a minute (relaxation time 66 ± 16 s).
source: Stress in gels relaxed to zero with a characteristic time constant on the scale of a minute (relaxation time 66 ± 16 s, mean ± SEM, N = 4 gels).
evidence: Supported by stress relaxation measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: 23% compression of single malignant cells led to reduction in colony size.
source: (C) 23% compression of single malignant cells led to reduction in colony size (N = 5, 9 pairs of gels, bars are mean ± SEM, points are means of individual experiments, with 90 ± 44 colonies per sample [mean ± SD]). *Difference is significant at p<0.05 in paired t-test, comparing compressed and uncompressed samples in same chamber preparation (see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C with statistical analysis (p<0.05).

claim: Colonies grown from compressed single cells exhibited enhanced growth arrest as determined by the absence of Ki67 stain.
source: (D) Colonies grown from compressed single cells exhibited enhanced growth arrest (N = 4, 4, 14, and 6 gels, mean ± SEM, with 33 ± 12 colonies per sample [mean ± SD]), determined by the absence of Ki67 stain. *Difference is statistically significant at p<0.02 in two-sample t-test.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis (p<0.02).

claim: With compression, the majority of T4-2 cells grew into smaller, more organized colonies which were similar to those treated with an inhibitor for epidermal growth factor receptor (Tyrphostin, AG 1478) or PI3K (LY294002).
source: With compression, the majority of T4-2 cells grew into smaller, more organized colonies which were similar to those treated with an inhibitor for epidermal growth factor receptor (Tyrphostin, AG 1478) or PI3K (LY294002) (Figure 1B–iii and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-iii and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The increase in the proportion of colonies with an organized phenotype and the decrease in proportion of a disorganized phenotype demonstrate that a fraction of the population of malignant T4-2 cells were phenotypically reverted with compression.
source: The increase in the proportion of colonies with an organized phenotype and the decrease in proportion of a disorganized phenotype in demonstrate that a fraction of the population of malignant T4-2 cells were phenotypically reverted with compression. This difference is statistically significant (*) between the T4-2 uncompressed and compressed (p<0.05, two-sample t-test, N = 3, 3 experiments).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis (p<0.05).
